use_case: Online sensor health monitoring
incurred_insecurity: Undetected sensor degradation creates latent failures in safety-critical measurement channels and safeguards instrumentation, undermining defense-in-depth and enabling adversaries to mask diversion or sabotage activities during monitoring blind spots. Operator reliance on AI health verdicts—combined with alarm fatigue or complacency—erodes manual cross-checking, while adversarial compromise of training data or model supply chains can systematically blind entire facility fleets to specific failure signatures an attacker plans to exploit.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Online sensor health monitoring is a critical safety and safeguards function that underpins nearly every automated decision in a nuclear facility. From an operations standpoint, if the AI system falsely declares sensors healthy when they are degrading, operators lose their window to perform preventive maintenance before those instruments fail during a transient or accident scenario—violating defense-in-depth by creating latent failures in measurement channels that are assumed available in safety analyses. Conversely, excessive false alarms erode operator trust and can lead to ignoring genuine health warnings or disabling the monitoring system entirely (automation disuse). In enrichment and reprocessing, sensor health directly affects material accountancy and safeguards: if flow, level, or radiation detectors drift undetected, material balance discrepancies grow unnoticed until they exceed detection thresholds, and an adversary could exploit that drift window to mask diversion. The AI's training data likely comes from normal operation with few genuine failure signatures, so it may fail to recognize novel degradation modes in new equipment or after design changes, and any cloud-connected inference path introduces a supply-chain risk where poisoned models could be deployed fleet-wide.

ai_engineer.argument: Online sensor health monitoring in nuclear facilities relies on ML models trained to detect anomalies in sensor behavior (drift, calibration error, incipient failure) across heterogeneous instrumentation fleets. The core ML fragility is data provenance and operational drift: models trained on simulated or lab-bench sensor degradation profiles may fail to generalize to field conditions where environmental stressors, aging mechanisms, and multi-sensor correlation patterns differ from training. Inference-time non-determinism in ensemble or Bayesian health classifiers creates repeatability challenges for regulatory compliance, and model updates propagate across facility fleets without per-site qualification. The architecture itself — often using transfer learning from one sensor type to another or relying on limited failure-mode exemplars — is vulnerable to low base-rate events (rare failure signatures) and concept drift as new sensor generations or operating regimes emerge.

security_specialist.argument: Online sensor health monitoring AI creates a critical adversarial opportunity: an attacker who can subtly compromise the model or its training data can mask real sensor degradation that would otherwise trigger human investigation, effectively blinding operators to precursor conditions the adversary plans to exploit. This is a high-value target because it's a trust concentrator—operators will rely on AI's 'healthy' verdict to not inspect physical instruments, and the system runs continuously with minimal human-in-the-loop verification. A sophisticated adversary (state-level or advanced insider) could use this as an enabling step: poison the model to ignore specific signatures (vibration, temperature, pressure anomalies) that their planned sabotage or diversion would produce, then execute the primary attack while the monitoring system provides false assurance. The use case spans power generation, enrichment, and reprocessing—domains where undetected sensor failure or adversary-induced blindness directly enables material diversion, equipment damage for later exploitation, or operational disruption timed to other facility vulnerabilities. Even non-adversarial model drift or data-quality failure becomes a security issue here, because an adversary can time their action to coincide with naturally degraded detection capability that no one notices.

incurred_insecurity: Undetected equipment degradation can lead to through-wall leaks, pressure boundary failures, or catastrophic ruptures in systems handling radioactive materials, fissile inventories, or corrosive reprocessing chemicals. An adversary who manipulates training data, inference inputs, or the model itself can mask visible structural weaknesses, timing sabotage around hidden defects that appear as accidental failures. Systematic false positives erode operator trust, causing real defects to be dismissed, while automation complacency and skill fade degrade the defense-in-depth principle that requires independent human verification. nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case directly influences whether operators detect safety-critical degradation before it leads to leaks, failures, or releases in active nuclear systems handling radioactive materials or high-energy fluids. If the AI misses genuine cracks (false negative), operators may defer maintenance on failing piping until catastrophic rupture; if it generates false positives or hallucinates damage, they may waste time or shut down healthy systems unnecessarily, eroding trust and potentially causing real defects to be ignored later. The model must generalize across diverse materials, lighting, surface conditions, and degradation modes (fatigue, corrosion, embrittlement) that vary by facility type—data from one enrichment cascade's stainless piping may not cover the corrosion mechanisms in reprocessing acid lines or the neutron-embrittlement signatures in power-reactor pressure boundaries. Operators acting on these recommendations lack transparency into why the AI flagged a region, making it difficult to cross-check against engineering judgment, and any adversarial manipulation of input imagery (or poisoned training data embedding benign-looking cracks) could systematically blind the system to real hazards.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case relies on multi-modal visual inputs (thermal, camera, possibly ultrasonic imaging) to detect degradation in safety-critical components across diverse nuclear facilities. The core ML fragility is concept drift: cracks/corrosion patterns evolve with aging fleet materials, new alloys in next-gen plants, and environmental stressors not seen during training (like accelerated degradation in unique reprocessing chemistries or waste-storage radiation fields). Training data is almost certainly bench-test or early-life operational data—realistic late-life degradation signatures, especially rare failure modes, are scarce because destructive validation destroys the very samples needed. At inference time, if the model encounters a novel crack morphology (intergranular vs. transgranular in a new alloy) or multi-modal misalignment (thermal/visual sensors out of sync), it may confidently misclassify benign wear as safe or miss incipient failure, with no mechanism to flag out-of-distribution uncertainty. Cross-facility deployment amplifies this: a model trained on PWR piping may confidently hallucinate 'no defect' when applied to reprocessing tankage with entirely different metallurgy and stress regimes.

damage.why: Undetected equipment degradation in pressure boundaries or containment systems handling radioactive materials can lead directly to through-wall leaks, loss-of-coolant events, or radiological release—the highest consequence category in this domain.

reproducibility.why: Once the described conditions are present (out-of-distribution inputs, concept drift, or adversarial manipulation), the vulnerability class reliably manifests as systematic false negatives or misclassifications, though some operational variability in imaging conditions exists.

exploitability.why: The vulnerability class spans a range: some mechanisms (adversarial image perturbation, training data poisoning) require insider access or supply-chain position, while others (out-of-distribution drift, multi-modal misalignment) can be triggered by routine operational heterogeneity without deliberate adversarial action.

affected_users.why: Failure propagates across multiple safety-critical systems (piping, pressure vessels, containment) and can impact facility-wide maintenance decisions, though typically scoped to equipment classes rather than causing immediate cascading failures across all coupled systems.

discoverability.why: Model diagnoses can be trialled on known hardware during staging. Basic pipework, acoustic signals can be easily recreated.

use_case: Material accounting (e.g. molten salt fuels, fluid reprocessing streams, spent fuel stocks)
incurred_insecurity: Failure or manipulation of AI-based fluid material accounting directly enables covert diversion of special nuclear material by degrading near-real-time detection of discrepancies in continuous, un-itemized streams where traditional discrete-item counting is unavailable. An adversary can exploit training data biases, undetected model drift, or operator over-reliance to mask kilogram-scale losses as measurement noise or acceptable variance, undermining the fundamental safeguards barrier and inspector confidence in material unaccounted-for (MUF) declarations.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Material accounting for fluid/dynamic fissile streams (molten salt, aqueous reprocessing solutions) is a safeguards-critical function where continuous mass-balance closure is the principal detection mechanism for diversion or unaccounted material. An AI system performing anomaly detection, predictive mass balancing, or automated reconciliation on streaming sensor data (flow, density, spectroscopy) directly informs MC&A declarations and near-real-time loss detection; if it fails to flag a genuine discrepancy or flags spurious anomalies that desensitize operators, the facility loses timely material unaccounted-for (MUF) visibility. Unlike solid fuel where item counting provides a hard boundary, fluid streams rely on integrating noisy/drifting sensor feeds over time, so data quality gaps, model drift as process chemistry evolves, and the small-data problem for protactinium or minor-actinide signatures in novel cycles all degrade detection sensitivity. Training on simulated fluid dynamics or lab-scale chemistry rather than full hot-cell data introduces a qualification gap that may not surface until the first real campaign, and any adversarial manipulation (poisoning training data to normalize small systematic losses, evading the model by exploiting known sensor blind spots) directly enables theft scenarios that traditional batch accountability would catch.

nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Failure or manipulation of AI-based fluid material accounting degrades the facility's ability to detect diversion or loss in near-real-time, directly enabling theft of special nuclear material if the discrepancy falls below the detection threshold or is masked by false negatives. ai_engineer.argument: Material accounting for molten salt or fluid reprocessing streams presents a severe data provenance problem: training data for these continuous, dynamic chemistries is virtually nonexistent in real operational contexts, forcing reliance on simulated or lab-scale surrogates that may not capture transient behaviors, chemical interactions, or sensor noise profiles seen in actual hot cells. The model must infer composition or mass balance from indirect measurements (gamma spectroscopy, density, flow rates) that are themselves noisy and subject to drift as sensors degrade in harsh radiation/chemical environments, yet any concept drift—changes in feed composition, process upset conditions, or sensor calibration states not seen during training—can silently degrade accuracy without obvious alarms. Because this is a continuous inference task, non-determinism at inference time (if the architecture uses stochastic elements or if sensor fusion weights fluctuate) undermines repeatability of material balance closure, making it impossible to distinguish genuine discrepancies (diversion indicators) from model artifacts. The operational consequence is that safeguards-critical material unaccounted for (MUF) calculations become untrustworthy: operators may either dismiss real anomalies as model noise (disuse) or accept spurious alerts as ground truth (misuse), and regulators cannot verify that the AI's material balance closure meets statutory thresholds because the system's decision boundary is opaque and its performance envelope on out-of-distribution transients is uncharacterized.

security_specialist.argument: Material accounting for molten salts or fluid reprocessing streams is a safeguards-critical function where an adversary gains enormous leverage if they can bias or blind the AI's mass-balance estimates—this is a direct path to covert diversion because fluid streams lack the discrete-item accountability of solid fuel. From a security lens, this use case creates a concentrated trust point: if an insider can subtly poison training data (perhaps by feeding biased calibration measurements over time) or exploit model drift (where the AI stops flagging small but persistent imbalances as the process ages), they effectively create a 'blind spot' in the accountancy system that a diversion operation can be timed around. The AI's opacity and the difficulty of qualifying it against low-base-rate diversion scenarios (OP.C0701) mean that an adversary doesn't need to hack the model directly—they can simply wait for natural drift or data-quality erosion to open a window, then exploit the operators' automation trust to avoid triggering manual cross-checks. Unlike static solid-fuel accounting, fluid systems depend on continuous sensor fusion and predictive modeling, so any compromise (or un-detected drift) in that AI pipeline directly erodes the facility's ability to detect even kilogram-scale losses, which is safeguards-significant.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged strongly on training data inadequacy (simulated/lab-scale vs. operational), sensor/concept drift, model opacity blocking regulatory verification, and the dual misuse/disuse risk where operators either dismiss real alerts or accept spurious ones. The security specialist's emphasis on adversarial exploitation (poisoning, insider calibration manipulation, timing diversions around drift) was integrated as distinct attack vectors rather than duplicating the nuclear engineer's detection-degradation framing. Items like 'hallucinatory material balance closure' and 'goal misalignment' from the nuclear engineer were retained as distinct from general opacity concerns; 'model extraction' and 'supply chain compromise' from the security specialist were kept as unique threat vectors not raised by others.

The concentration of material accountancy trust in AI outputs creates a single point of compromise that erodes traditional independent verification disciplines.

nuclear_engineer.argument: In reprocessing and waste facilities, spent fuel characterization directly informs criticality safety calculations, safeguards accountancy declarations, and waste classification decisions. If the AI mischaracterizes burn-up or isotopic composition—whether through operational drift as fuel types evolve, data poisoning of measurement feeds, or evasion where an adversary deliberately presents atypical material—operators may unknowingly batch incompatible assemblies, underreport plutonium inventories, or mis-classify high-activity waste streams. Existing procedural controls (independent sampling, cross-instrument verification, mass balance reconciliation) are designed to catch gross discrepancies, but automation bias can erode those layers if staff treat AI output as authoritative without challenge. The consequence is not just a paperwork error: criticality margin violations or diverted fissile material represent direct safety and safeguards failures that emerge only after the AI's characterization has already guided irreversible physical operations.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Incorrect fuel characterization can lead operators to violate criticality safety margins during batch assembly, misreport accountancy to safeguards authorities enabling diversion pathways, or misclassify waste streams causing downstream handling or disposal hazards. These failures materialise only after physical fuel movements or declarations have been executed based on flawed AI output.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case relies on training data derived from known fuel histories (burn-up, enrichment, isotopic signatures) that may not represent adversarial scenarios such as deliberate material substitution, undeclared irradiation cycles, or clandestine blending of fuel batches. The model's ability to detect 'missing material' presumes that training examples captured the spectral or physical signatures of partial diversion, yet such ground-truth labels are rare and may be synthetically generated or based on simulations rather than real diversion events. At inference, if an actor presents spent fuel with isotopic ratios engineered to mimic a declared history (evasion), the system may confidently classify it within its trained manifold despite the deception. Data provenance is critical: if the training set lacks examples of certain enrichment routes, reprocessing techniques, or reactor types now appearing in the operational environment, the model will extrapolate unreliably. Retraining cycles must account for evolving fuel cycle technologies and adversarial tactics, yet the lag between operational deployment and model updates creates a window where novel material characteristics fall outside the trained scope.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: An attacker could present engineered spent fuel assemblies whose isotopic or physical signatures were crafted to evade detection of diversion or undeclared irradiation, exploiting the model's reliance on historical training distributions that lack adversarial examples. Operational drift in fuel cycle technologies or enrichment pathways not represented in training data would cause the system to misclassify novel material characteristics, enabling safeguards circumvention.

security_specialist.argument: An adversary seeking to divert material from reprocessing or falsify waste inventories would find this AI system an attractive target for data poisoning or evasion attacks. If the AI's training data or input measurements can be subtly manipulated—perhaps by an insider with access to gamma spectroscopy feeds or declared facility records—the system could be made to systematically underreport fissile content, misattribute isotopic ratios to lower-value material, or fail to flag missing assemblies. The concentration of material accountancy trust in an AI classifier creates a single point of compromise: unlike traditional cross-checks by independent human inspectors using different methods, a well-targeted data integrity attack here could simultaneously fool both operator and safeguards inspector if both rely on the same AI-generated characterization. Nation-state adversaries with advanced technical capabilities could pre-position dormant data-poisoning payloads during procurement or training phases, activated only when diversion operations commence, making attribution and detection exceedingly difficult.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Creates a high-value single point of compromise for material accountancy, where adversarial manipulation of training data or runtime inputs could enable undetected diversion at reprocessing facilities or inventory fraud in waste streams, with operator/inspector reliance on AI outputs eroding traditional independent verification discipline.

use_case: Corrective action suggestion (e.g. for coincident alarms)
incurred_insecurity: Incorrect corrective actions during coincident alarms could disable safety systems, delay needed mitigations, or mask escalating faults—including sabotage or diversion scenarios—if operators defer to AI suggestions without independent verification of plant state, particularly when novel transients or adversarial manipulation produce plausible but incorrect recommendations.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Corrective action suggestions during coincident alarms are high-pressure operational moments where operators must quickly discern whether multiple alarms reflect a single root cause or independent failures. If the AI misdiagnoses the situation—whether through model drift as plant aging changes alarm signatures, or through misaligned output that confuses symptom with cause—operators may execute incorrect mitigating actions (e.g., isolating a functioning system or failing to isolate an actual fault). Automation bias is a severe concern here: operators under cognitive load may defer to the AI's suggestion without cross-checking physical plant parameters or conducting the structured diagnostic reasoning that procedures require. Existing defense-in-depth (independent confirmation channels, procedure adherence, supervisory oversight) provides partial mitigation, but only if operators recognize the AI as advisory rather than directive—a distinction that erodes with repeated 'successful' suggestions.

nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Incorrect corrective actions during coincident alarms could disable safety systems, delay needed mitigations, or mask escalating faults, directly challenging defense-in-depth if operators override procedural reasoning in favor of AI suggestions without independent verification of plant state.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case relies on multi-modal sensor fusion (alarms, instrumentation, operational state) to recommend corrective actions in real-time during potentially abnormal conditions. The training corpus likely drew from historical alarm patterns and resolved incidents, but coincident alarms during novel transients—especially at enrichment or reprocessing facilities with unique process chemistries—may fall outside the distribution the model saw. If the model was trained on power-generation operational data and then transfer-learned to enrichment cascades, the feature space (pressure transients in centrifuges vs. coolant loops) and fault signatures differ fundamentally, risking incorrect action recommendations. Operators under time pressure may exhibit automation bias, trusting a confident but hallucinated suggestion during a scenario the model never encountered in training.

ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Operators receive plausible but incorrect corrective actions during novel or cross-domain fault scenarios (e.g., enrichment cascade pressure spikes misclassified as analogous reactor coolant events), potentially causing equipment damage, material loss, or criticality concerns if the suggested action exacerbates the underlying fault condition.

security_specialist.argument: An adversary with insider access could exploit the corrective action suggestion system as a trust anchor to manipulate operator response during a coordinated attack. By subtly poisoning training data or exploiting operational drift over time, an attacker could condition the system to suggest benign-seeming actions during specific alarm signatures that actually mask sabotage or facilitate material diversion. The system creates a single point of influence: if operators develop automation bias and defer to AI suggestions during high-stress coincident alarm scenarios, an adversary can time physical actions (valve manipulation, material removal) to coincide with periods when the AI provides cover by suggesting 'normal' corrective steps. This is particularly valuable in enrichment and reprocessing facilities where alarm patterns associated with diversion could be reframed by the AI as routine operational transients requiring standard corrections.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The corrective action system becomes a high-value target for adversarial compromise because it directly shapes operator decision-making during the exact scenarios (coincident alarms) that could indicate sabotage or diversion, effectively allowing an attacker to 'speak through' the trusted AI to misdirect human response at critical moments.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on automation bias and operational drift as core vulnerabilities during high-pressure alarm response. The nuclear and AI engineers both identified model/distribution issues (drift, transfer mismatch, novel scenarios), while the security specialist uniquely highlighted adversarial exploitation via data poisoning—a distinct attack vector that leverages the same automation bias the others identified defensively. use_case: Fault severity classification and prioritization
incurred_insecurity: Misclassification of fault severity—whether due to training-data gaps, real-time adversarial manipulation, or operational drift—can lead operators to defer protective actions on genuine critical faults or waste resources chasing false alarms, eroding both safety margins and operational trust. Adversaries may exploit the centralized trust in AI triage to suppress detection of sabotage or degradation, while automation bias reduces independent operator vigilance during novel or compound fault scenarios.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Fault severity classification systems inform immediate operational decisions—whether to continue operation, initiate a controlled shutdown, or trigger emergency protocols. If the AI misclassifies a severe fault as benign (false negative), operators may delay protective actions, allowing degradation of safety barriers or loss of containment boundaries. Conversely, false positives that over-classify routine anomalies create alarm fatigue and resource misallocation, eroding trust in genuine alerts. In enrichment and reprocessing facilities, misclassification could mask criticality-related instrument drift or material accountancy discrepancies that require immediate safeguards response. Existing practice relies on redundant instrumentation and independent verification by licensed operators, but automation bias may lead personnel to defer to AI prioritization without applying traditional engineering judgment, especially during high-tempo or complex transient conditions.

nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Operators may accept incorrect fault severity rankings during novel transients or degraded-equipment scenarios not represented in training data, bypassing procedural requirements for independent verification and allowing safety-significant conditions to persist unmitigated or diverting resources from genuine emergent threats.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case centers on a classifier that ingests sensor/diagnostic data and outputs a severity label plus priority ranking. From a pipeline perspective, the primary fragility is at inference time: if real faults present with symptom patterns (sensor signatures, failure modes, timing) not well-represented in the training corpus, the model will misclassify severity or assign incorrect priority. Training data for fault classification in nuclear facilities is inherently sparse and imbalanced—catastrophic failures are rare, so the model likely over-fits to benign or moderate events and under-represents novel or compound fault signatures. Data drift is also acute: as equipment ages, sensors degrade, and operational profiles shift (e.g., power-uprate, fuel-type changes), the input distribution diverges from what the model saw during training, eroding classification accuracy precisely when operators need it most. Finally, reliance on operator-reported labels or legacy maintenance logs introduces label noise and potential negative bias (e.g., under-reporting low-consequence events in certain facility types), skewing the learned severity boundaries.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: unique failure modes outside trained scope
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Misclassification at inference (low-severity label on a genuinely critical fault, or vice versa) directly leads to mis-prioritized maintenance queues: critical hazards may be deferred while resources chase false alarms, degrading both safety margin and operational efficiency in the facility.

security_specialist.argument: A fault classification AI becomes a high-value target for an adversary seeking to mask malicious activity or induce operational chaos. An insider or external actor who gains access to the model's input pathway could craft synthetic fault signatures that the AI systematically misclassifies as low-priority, allowing genuine sabotage or degradation to progress undetected while operators trust the AI's triage. Alternatively, poisoning the training data or model updates over time could shift the classifier's decision boundary such that critical precursors to a engineered failure event are downgraded, creating a window for coordinated attack. The trust placed in automated prioritization erodes the vigilance of human operators who might otherwise catch anomalous patterns, and the system's existence consolidates decision authority in a way that rewards compromise—flipping one model is more efficient than deceiving multiple independent human analysts across shifts.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Adversaries gain a leverage point to suppress detection of deliberate component degradation or sabotage by manipulating how faults are ranked, while operator over-reliance on AI triage masks the attack until damage is irreversible or an incident window opens.

use_case: Autonomous and semi-autonomous control
incurred_insecurity: Autonomous control bypasses traditional human verification loops, allowing model degradation, adversarial manipulation, or training-inference mismatch to propagate directly into safety-critical actuations (reactivity control, cascade pressures, process chemistry) before operators or procedural safeguards can intervene. This creates a concentrated attack surface where insiders or sophisticated adversaries can exploit operational drift, data integrity failures, or reduced operator vigilance to manipulate physical processes toward unsafe or safeguards-relevant states across multiple facility domains.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Autonomous or semi-autonomous control in power generation, enrichment, or reprocessing facilities creates an operational safety concern when AI actuation occurs faster than human intervention loops or when operators over-rely on AI correctness without independent verification. In nuclear facilities, control actions directly affect critical safety parameters—reactor power, coolant flow, centrifuge cascade pressures, or chemical process temperatures—where incorrect actuation can challenge safety limits before procedural safeguards trigger. If operators become complacent and fail to maintain situational awareness or questioning attitude, they may not recognize when the AI system has drifted from safe operational envelopes due to changing plant conditions, sensor degradation, or unanticipated transients. The physical actuation authority granted to these systems means that model drift, operational drift, or adversarial manipulation translates directly into control actions that bypass traditional human-in-the-loop barriers, compressing the time available for recovery.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Autonomous control bypasses traditional human verification loops, allowing incorrect AI outputs to directly actuate safety-critical systems (reactivity control, process chemistry, pressure boundaries) before operators or procedural safeguards can intervene, potentially challenging technical safety limits or safeguards material accountability.

ai_engineer.argument: Autonomous or semi-autonomous control systems in nuclear operations present severe ML pipeline vulnerabilities centered on training-inference mismatch and actuator-level attack surface. These systems must generalize across highly heterogeneous facility designs (power reactors, enrichment cascades, reprocessing hot cells) where edge cases in the operational envelope are neither rare nor benign—control inputs outside the distribution seen during training can lead directly to unsafe actuation. The reliance on operational sensor streams means data drift (sensor degradation, calibration drift, novel transient signatures) erodes model validity over time, yet the retraining and re-qualification loop for safety-critical control is glacially slow. The architecture itself creates a direct path from data manipulation or adversarial input at inference time to physical actuation, making this use case uniquely fragile at the model-to-actuator boundary where traditional software V&V ends and ML uncertainty begins.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: unique failure modes outside trained scope
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Model degradation due to sensor drift or novel operational states can propagate undetected into control commands, while the direct coupling between inference outputs and physical actuators creates an attack surface where data integrity failures or adversarial inputs bypass traditional interlock logic and translate into unsafe facility states before human intervention is possible.

security_specialist.argument: Autonomous or semi-autonomous control systems in power generation, enrichment, or reprocessing facilities create a high-value concentration point for adversarial targeting: compromise of the control logic or its trust chain allows an insider or sophisticated external attacker to manipulate safety-critical or safeguards-relevant processes while appearing to operate within normal parameters. The system's ability to act on its own decisions means an adversary can pre-position malicious behavior that executes without immediate human confirmation, exploiting the facility's reliance on AI-mediated situational awareness to mask sabotage or diversion until damage is irreversible. Unlike passive monitoring tools, autonomous control represents a physical actuation pathway; if an adversary can inject evasive inputs or exploit the AI's operational boundaries (e.g., scenarios outside its training), they can steer centrifuge cascades, coolant flows, or chemical separations toward unsafe or proliferation-relevant states. The insider threat dimension is acute: operators with legitimate access to the control AI's configuration, training data, or operational parameters can subtly bias its decision-making (data poisoning, prompt injecting via maintenance interfaces) to create windows of vulnerability timed to external coordination.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: An adversary—whether insider or sophisticated external actor—gains a scalable, potentially covert means to manipulate safety-critical or safeguards-relevant physical processes across multiple facility types, with reduced operator vigilance and expanded windows for undetected sabotage or diversion.

use_case: Cybersecurity (e.g. intrusion detection)
incurred_insecurity: Adversaries can systematically evade detection by probing the AI's learned boundaries, poisoning training data to exclude their signatures, or timing intrusions around model update cycles, while operator complacency from frequent false positives or misplaced trust in the AI erodes manual vigilance. This allows attackers to establish persistence, move laterally across networks, and position themselves to exfiltrate safeguards data or manipulate control systems before human defenders recognize the breach.

nuclear_engineer.argument: In plant operations, intrusion detection systems (IDS) serve as a critical early-warning layer, but operators rely on accurate, timely alerts to distinguish genuine cyber threats from false positives. If an AI-based IDS suffers from evasion—where adversaries craft network traffic to slip past the model's learned signatures—or from operational drift as the facility's legitimate network baseline evolves (new equipment, updated protocols), the system may fail silently or flood operators with false alarms. Complacency sets in when operators habitually dismiss frequent false positives, exactly when a real intrusion occurs. Existing procedural controls (defense-in-depth, air-gapped safety systems, manual oversight of critical commands) may still prevent physical harm, but the AI failure degrades the very cybersecurity posture it was meant to enhance, allowing adversaries persistence or lateral movement before detection.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Missed or delayed detection of cyber intrusions undermines defense-in-depth, permitting adversaries to establish persistence, exfiltrate sensitive operational or safeguards data, or position themselves for subsequent manipulation of process control or safety systems before human operators recognize the breach.

ai_engineer.argument: Intrusion detection systems for nuclear facilities rely on models trained against historical attack patterns and normal operational baselines, creating acute exposure to 'security landscape drift' as threat actors evolve tactics faster than retraining cycles. The training data provenance is critical: if the model was trained on IT network telemetry from conventional enterprises rather than OT/ICS traffic specific to enrichment cascades or reactor control systems, it will exhibit 'dataset bias' and fail to recognize nuclear-specific attack vectors (e.g., attempts to manipulate centrifuge frequency controls or poison isotope assay data). At inference time, novel attack strategies—particularly those designed to appear as legitimate maintenance actions or calibration drift—constitute 'evasion' because the model has no historical exemplars of adversarial behavior tailored to nuclear process control. The retraining pipeline itself becomes a vulnerability: incorporating adversarial examples without rigorous provenance checking enables 'data poisoning' where attackers subtly shift the decision boundary to exclude their own intrusion signatures.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The ML pipeline's dependence on static training distributions and lagging retraining cadence means sophisticated attackers can systematically probe and evade detection boundaries, while poisoned training updates can blind the system to entire classes of nuclear-targeted intrusions before any facility-level control failure occurs.

security_specialist.argument: An AI intrusion detection system creates a single point of adversarial interest: if an attacker can characterize its detection boundaries (through probing, insider knowledge of model updates, or exfiltrated training data), they gain a predictable evasion roadmap that would not exist with unpredictable human analyst rotation. The system's reliance on historical data means a patient adversary—particularly a nation-state with multi-year timelines—can subtly poison the baseline through low-and-slow reconnaissance that gets labeled as 'normal,' causing the model to drift toward accepting malicious patterns. Furthermore, deploying this at enrichment or reprocessing facilities means adversaries may prioritize compromising the AI's update pipeline or training corpus over the control systems themselves, as a successfully evaded IDS grants freedom of maneuver across the entire digital estate. Operator complacency is the force multiplier: if security staff trust the AI's silence as confirmation of safety rather than maintaining independent vigilance, an adversary can time kinetic or cyber actions during model retraining windows, shift changes, or known false-negative conditions.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: A sophisticated adversary gains a learnable, exploitable gatekeeper: by mapping the AI's detection envelope and timing attacks around model update cycles or poisoned baselines, they can move through the facility's networks undetected while security personnel atrophy their manual vigilance, trusting the AI's silence as assurance rather than a manipulated blindspot.

use_case: Manual summarization and distillation
incurred_insecurity: Personnel may act on AI-generated summaries containing omitted, distorted, or fabricated operational details without independent verification, potentially leading to incorrect procedures or deferred inspections. Additionally, the summarization function provides a low-signature pathway for insiders to aggregate compartmentalized safety protocols, physical protection details, and procedural dependencies across controlled documents, enabling reconnaissance that traditional access auditing would not detect.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Manual summarization and distillation of operational and maintenance documentation, procedures, or data logs creates critical reliance on AI-generated condensed information that operators or engineers will use for decision-making. If the AI misattributes findings, omits safety-critical details, or hallucinates plausible-sounding but incorrect conditions (e.g., misrepresenting a trending parameter or conflating maintenance schedules across different systems), downstream personnel may act on incomplete or fabricated summaries without cross-checking source material. Operators accustomed to trustworthy human-generated summaries may exhibit automation bias, failing to independently verify AI distillations before executing equipment isolation, mode changes, or maintenance activities. Existing procedural safeguards—independent verification, peer checks, or mandatory reference to controlled documents—would need to erode or be bypassed for this to cause physical consequences, but time pressure during outages or high workload periods increases that risk.

nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Personnel acting on AI-summarized operational or maintenance information may unknowingly execute incorrect sequences, apply inappropriate technical specifications, or defer critical inspections if the model omits, distorts, or fabricates procedural details, degrading defense-in-depth when independent verification is not enforced.

ai_engineer.argument: Manual summarization and distillation of operational/maintenance documentation across diverse facility domains (power generation, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication) is highly sensitive to training data coverage and domain-specific terminology. Large language models trained on general or even nuclear-specific corpora may lack representation of facility-specific procedures, vendor-proprietary acronyms, or site-unique operational contexts, leading to hallucinations or incorrect attributions when summarizing critical maintenance steps or safety protocols. The inference pipeline has no ground-truth verification loop—outputs are text summaries that operators must trust without easy validation. Multi-use acronyms (e.g., 'MOX' for mixed-oxide fuel vs. other industrial/military uses, 'RCS' for reactor coolant system vs. revision control system) create a concrete failure mode where the model misattributes context, especially when distilling cross-domain documents. Data provenance is a significant risk: if training included publicly scraped technical forums or unvetted vendor manuals, the model may propagate outdated procedures or conflate similar-but-distinct processes across enrichment vs. reprocessing workflows.

This is compounded by the model's inability to signal when input documentation falls outside its training distribution (e.g., a novel fuel fabrication process or site-specific retrofit procedure), leading to silent failures in the text output that propagate into operational decision-making.

security_specialist.argument: Manual summarization of operational and maintenance documentation (procedures, logs, incident reports, training materials) across sensitive fuel-cycle facilities creates a concentrated information-disclosure pathway that an insider or compromised account could exploit without triggering traditional document-access audits. An adversary could craft queries to extract safety margins, emergency response protocols, or physical protection system details that are normally compartmentalized across multiple controlled documents, effectively using the AI as an unmonitored aggregation oracle. The summarization function's design assumes benign use, but a sophisticated attacker would use it to map vulnerabilities (e.g., which maintenance windows disable redundant safeguards, which alarm setpoints are considered nuisance versus critical) that inform physical or cyber attack timing. use_case: Predictive maintenance and remaining useful life estimation
incurred_insecurity: AI-driven predictive maintenance may fail to detect emerging component degradation when confronted with rare failure modes, site-specific physics, or adversarially manipulated sensor data, leading operators to defer critical inspections until catastrophic failure occurs. This risk is compounded by automation bias eroding manual verification practices and by data drift as operational envelopes evolve, potentially causing unplanned outages, confinement breaches, or enabling adversaries to time sabotage when component health is unknowingly degraded.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Predictive maintenance AI relies on historical sensor and operational data to forecast component degradation, but nuclear facilities exhibit unique failure modes tied to radiation damage, thermal cycling, and material embrittlement that may not generalize across sites or be well-represented in training data. If the model fails to recognize an emerging degradation pattern (e.g., stress-corrosion cracking in a fuel assembly mechanical component or unexpected wear in enrichment centrifuge bearings), maintenance could be deferred until catastrophic failure, potentially causing unplanned shutdowns, contamination events, or loss of material accountability. Operators trusting AI-generated remaining useful life estimates may bypass manual inspections or condition monitoring that would otherwise catch anomalies, creating a procedural safeguard gap. The consequence severity scales with facility type: in reprocessing, unexpected equipment failure could breach confinement barriers; in enrichment, rotor failure risks UF6 release and criticality concerns.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: unique failure modes outside trained scope
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Undetected component failures due to AI underestimating degradation rates or missing site-specific failure modes, leading to unplanned outages, breach of confinement, or loss of safeguards control if maintenance is improperly deferred based on flawed remaining useful life predictions.

ai_engineer.argument: Predictive maintenance models for remaining useful life (RUL) estimation rely on historical sensor time-series data that may not adequately capture rare degradation modes or component-specific failure signatures, especially across diverse facility types (enrichment centrifuges vs. reactor pumps vs. fuel pellet presses). The training dataset likely underrepresents edge cases—unusual operating regimes, novel failure modes, or components with sparse failure history—leading to overconfident RUL predictions when the model encounters unfamiliar degradation patterns at inference time. Data drift is inevitable as equipment ages, maintenance practices evolve, or operational envelopes shift (e.g., power uprates, feedstock changes in enrichment), yet the model may not be retrained frequently enough or with sufficient provenance over what changed. The architecture's generalization to the long tail of component-specific physics (thermal fatigue in one alloy vs. corrosion in another) is questionable without transfer-learning validation across sites, and reliance on operator-reported maintenance logs introduces data integrity risks if those logs are incomplete, delayed, or inconsistent in taxonomy.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: unique failure modes outside trained scope
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The model may fail to flag emerging failures or provide falsely optimistic RUL estimates when encountering degradation physics not represented in training data, leading to missed maintenance windows or unplanned outages. Over-reliance on stale or incomplete operator logs further degrades prediction fidelity, while drift between training and operational regimes erodes confidence without explicit requalification triggers.

security_specialist.argument: Predictive maintenance systems become trusted gatekeepers for which components receive scrutiny and which are deemed 'healthy,' creating an exploitable chokepoint. An insider or supply-chain compromiser could poison the sensor streams or model inputs to mask degradation in a target component (e.g., a centrifuge cascade seal, a fuel cladding integrity sensor, or a criticality alarm circuit), causing operators to defer inspection until catastrophic failure or until the adversary's preferred timing. Because these systems often gain privileged data access across multiple safety-critical and safeguards-relevant subsystems to correlate failure modes, compromising the predictive maintenance AI provides a surveillance platform for reconnaissance of facility health and operational tempo—intelligence valuable for timing a physical or cyber sabotage event when defenses are degraded. The operational trust placed in AI-driven maintenance scheduling erodes the culture of skeptical, hands-on verification that historically served as a defense-in-depth layer against both accidental and deliberate component failure.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: inability to detect unique or contrived component modifications
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: An adversary can covertly manipulate maintenance priorities to either hide sabotage-induced degradation or gain reconnaissance on facility-wide component health and inspection schedules, timing subsequent kinetic or cyber attacks when critical systems are unknowingly compromised and human vigilance has been algorithmically suppressed.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the core risks of unrepresented failure modes, data drift, and automation bias undermining human oversight. The security specialist's unique contribution on data poisoning and reconnaissance via privileged data access was retained as a distinct adversarial dimension, while 'operational drift' and 'sensitivity to transfer learning' were subsumed under the broader 'data drift' and 'unique failure modes' terms already covering those concerns.

use_case: Generate bespoke or individualized learning material

nuclear_engineer.argument: When AI generates individualized training material for nuclear operators, engineers, or safeguards personnel across diverse facility types (power, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication), the primary operational risk is that plausible-sounding but factually incorrect or incomplete content becomes embedded in institutional knowledge. If the AI hallucinates procedural steps, misattributes safety limits across facility domains, or oversimplifies complex engineering controls, trainees may internalize erroneous mental models that later manifest as procedural violations or missed abnormal conditions during actual operations. Existing training quality-assurance processes (instructor review, simulator validation, examination boards) are the primary defense, but bespoke AI-generated content at scale may bypass traditional peer review if organizations treat the AI as a subject-matter expert rather than a draft generator. The consequence is degraded human performance in safety-critical or safeguards-sensitive tasks, where the gap between what was taught and what is correct only surfaces during an actual transient, material accountancy discrepancy, or audit.

nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Operators and engineers trained on AI-generated material containing hallucinated procedures, misattributed safety limits, or facility-specific inaccuracies may execute incorrect actions during normal or off-normal conditions, bypassing the defense-in-depth provided by procedurally correct human performance and increasing reliance on remaining engineered safeguards to prevent safety or safeguards consequences.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case relies on a generative model (likely an LLM or fine-tuned variant) to produce training materials across highly specialized, safety-critical domains (enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, power generation). The core ML fragility is that the model's training corpus determines what it 'knows' about nuclear engineering workflows, and any gap between that corpus and the actual operational context of a specific facility becomes a direct pathway to incorrect or misleading content. If the model was trained predominantly on publicly available academic material or one regulatory regime's documentation, it will hallucinate or misattribute procedures when generating content for a facility operating under different standards, with different equipment lineages, or in a regulatory environment not well-represented in the training set. At inference time, there is no ground-truth feedback loop to catch fabricated references, subtly incorrect parameter ranges, or conflated procedures from different facility types—this is pure generative output with no runtime validation against actual operational data. The data provenance problem is acute: if the training set included outdated standards, contractor-specific jargon, or cross-contamination between civilian and research reactor documentation, those biases propagate directly into the learning materials without the model having any mechanism to flag uncertainty or domain boundaries.

security_specialist.argument: An AI training system that generates bespoke learning materials for nuclear facility operators creates a concentrated attack surface: compromise the generation pipeline once, and malicious content propagates to multiple trainees across sensitive facility types. security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Personalized AI-generated training materials become a high-value target for adversaries seeking to degrade operator competence or embed exploitable misconceptions at scale, while the system's aggregation of facility-specific learning needs creates actionable intelligence on workforce vulnerabilities and facility operations that would otherwise require extensive insider access to obtain.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Documentation retrieval and knowledge mining for training nuclear engineers and operators carries unique risks when AI outputs are misaligned, hallucinatory, or misattributed, because learners may internalize incorrect procedures, safety limits, or technical explanations before ever working in the field. If the AI retrieves or synthesizes guidance from the wrong facility type (e.g., BWR procedures presented for PWR training, or enrichment criticality controls applied to reprocessing scenarios), transfer-learning mismatch between sites can embed procedural errors that persist into operational practice. Additionally, multi-use acronyms common across power generation, enrichment, and reprocessing contexts—such as SG (steam generator vs. safeguards), MOX (mixed oxide fuel vs. material oxidation), or MPC (multi-purpose canister vs. material protection and control)—create mistranslation or misattribution risks that corrupt foundational knowledge. The consequence is not immediate plant impact, but erosion of the human knowledge base: operators and engineers trained on flawed AI-generated content may fail to recognize abnormal conditions, misapply limits, or bypass safeguards under the mistaken belief they are following correct doctrine.

ai_engineer.argument: Documentation retrieval systems for nuclear facilities typically rely on RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) architectures or embedding-based search over large heterogeneous corpora spanning decades of operational procedures, regulatory guidance, and vendor documentation. The core ML fragility here is that training embeddings or vector representations depend heavily on the corpus composition and version control: if the system is trained on a snapshot that excludes recent regulatory amendments, operational lessons learned, or facility-specific modifications, retrieval will systematically miss or deprioritize the most current or contextually relevant documents. At inference time, user queries may use domain-specific jargon, acronyms with multiple meanings across power generation, enrichment, and reprocessing contexts, or reference unique facility configurations not well-represented in the training corpus, causing the embedding distance metric to surface plausible-but-wrong documents. Additionally, if the generative component hallucinates citations or misattributes retrieved fragments to the wrong source document, operators may act on procedurally incorrect or outdated information without realizing the provenance is flawed.

ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Training-time corpus gaps and inference-time hallucination mean that operators may retrieve outdated procedures, misidentified regulatory guidance, or documents from the wrong facility domain, directly undermining the accuracy of knowledge transfer and increasing the likelihood of procedurally non-compliant or unsafe actions during training or operational decision-making.

security_specialist.argument: Documentation retrieval systems become high-value insider targets because they aggregate institutional knowledge that would otherwise require years of access to accumulate, and they create a queryable interface to sensitive process details across power generation, enrichment, and reprocessing domains. An adversary-recruited insider or compromised account could use seemingly innocuous queries to map facility-specific vulnerabilities, extract design rationale that reveals security assumptions, or identify which procedures rely on undocumented tribal knowledge versus written controls. The system's utility depends on indexing authentic facility documents, making it vulnerable to data poisoning where an adversary with document-submission privileges plants subtly altered procedures or reference materials that would surface during routine knowledge mining, establishing plausible deniability when operators later follow contaminated guidance. Most critically, centralizing retrieval erodes the natural compartmentalization where different expertise domains remain siloed—a junior operator in power generation should not trivially query reprocessing hold-up points or enrichment cascade control logic, yet the teaching function incentivizes broad access that an insider threat can exploit for reconnaissance far beyond their legitimate need-to-know.

incurred_insecurity: Adversaries or supply chain compromise can cause the AI authentication system to accept counterfeit, substandard, or maliciously modified components into safety-critical or safeguards-significant equipment, bypassing traditional multi-party verification and creating latent failure modes, undocumented diversion pathways, or intelligence-gathering opportunities. Simultaneously, operational drift or adversarial manipulation may cause rejection of legitimate suppliers, forcing manual overrides that erode trust in the protective system.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Supply chain authentication in nuclear construction relies on verifying that components—valves, pumps, instrumentation, reactor internals—are genuine, meet specification, and have not been tampered with or substituted. If an AI system authenticating supplier documentation, material certificates, or component provenance is compromised or produces incorrect output, operators or procurement staff may accept counterfeit, substandard, or maliciously altered parts into safety-critical or safeguards-significant systems. Existing quality assurance programs include receipt inspection, N-stamp certification, and traceability protocols, but these may be bypassed if personnel trust AI-flagged authenticity without independent verification. The consequence is that fraudulent components enter the facility undetected, potentially causing equipment failure (safety consequence) or enabling diversion pathways (safeguards consequence) if, for example, instrumentation is subtly modified.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: inability to detect unique or contrived component modifications
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Counterfeit, substandard, or maliciously modified components are accepted into safety systems or safeguards-significant equipment because AI authentication fails and procedural controls (receipt inspection, independent verification) are not enforced, leading to latent equipment failure modes or undocumented diversion pathways.

ai_engineer.argument: Supply chain authentication in nuclear contexts relies heavily on digitally verifiable provenance records (shipping manifests, certificates of origin, component serial numbers, supplier documentation) that an AI system must parse, cross-reference, and flag anomalies in. Adversaries can deliberately corrupt or inject malicious metadata into upstream supplier systems—what appears in training as a legitimate certificate format becomes a vector for data poisoning if an attacker controls even one node in the supply chain. The model's inference pipeline depends on data integrity at ingestion: if document formats, supplier identifiers, or cryptographic signatures are subtly altered (either maliciously or through operational drift as suppliers change ERP systems), the classifier may fail to recognize known-good suppliers or accept fraudulent ones. Because nuclear supply chains span decades and diverse international vendors, the training corpus cannot cover every future supplier's data schema or every adversarial forgery technique, leaving the system vulnerable to materials or documentation structures outside its trained scope.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Compromised provenance data or adversarial document injection can cause the authentication system to accept counterfeit or substandard components (enabling material substitution attacks) or reject legitimate suppliers (disrupting construction timelines and forcing manual overrides that undermine the AI's protective role).

security_specialist.argument: An AI system authenticating supply-chain provenance for nuclear components becomes an attractive target for credential theft or insider misuse because compromise converts it into a legitimization engine for counterfeit or substituted parts. A sophisticated adversary (state or proxy) could poison training data during development—feeding the model examples of known-good components that subtly include adversary-controlled suppliers—so that later insertion of malicious hardware appears authentic. The system also creates a single high-value choke point: if an insider or external attacker can manipulate the AI's output (evasion, prompt injection via embedded metadata in component documentation, or direct model tampering), they bypass traditional multi-party verification and inspection rituals that formerly distributed trust. Unlike random failure, an adversary will time component insertion to coincide with periods when operators are most reliant on the AI's verdict (e.g., urgent outage repairs), exploiting the automation bias that develops when the system has a long record of correct decisions.

use_case: Robotics and remote handling
incurred_insecurity: AI-driven robotic systems during construction can embed permanent physical defects in safety-critical structures, containment barriers, or safeguards equipment through inference failures or adversarial manipulation. These errors may remain undetected through commissioning, creating latent vulnerabilities that defeat downstream safety barriers during operations or provide adversaries a credential-mediated sabotage pathway without physical access to controlled areas.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Robotics and remote handling in design and construction phases involve physical actuation systems positioning equipment, manipulating components, and performing critical assembly or installation tasks across diverse facility types. If AI-driven path planning or manipulation algorithms produce incorrect commands—whether from operational drift between facility environments, unique failure modes in novel equipment configurations, or adversarial manipulation—the robot could physically damage safety-critical structures, misposition shielding or containment barriers, or create geometric misalignments that compromise future safeguards effectiveness. Unlike operational settings where process interlocks might catch errors, construction phases often rely on human verification of completed work, meaning incorrect robotic execution could persist undetected until commissioning or even operational upset. The physical actuation attack surface is particularly concerning because a single manipulation error during construction (e.g., incorrect welding parameter, misaligned fuel handling equipment) can create latent vulnerabilities that defeat multiple downstream safety barriers.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: unique failure modes outside trained scope
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Robotic construction errors could embed permanent physical defects in safety systems, containment structures, or safeguards equipment that remain undetected until they defeat critical barriers during operations. A single AI-commanded actuation mistake during installation creates a latent vulnerability that human inspection protocols may not identify before the facility is energized or loaded with nuclear material.

ai_engineer.argument: Robotics and remote handling systems for design and construction in power, enrichment, and reprocessing facilities depend heavily on vision models, kinematics planning, and sensor fusion trained on specific environmental conditions and object geometries. The training data provenance is critical: if the system was trained on simulated CAD environments or a limited set of construction scenarios, real-world variability in lighting, occlusions, material textures, or unexpected geometries can cause catastrophic misclassification or path-planning failures at inference time. Operational drift is almost guaranteed as facility layouts evolve during construction phases, materials are substituted, or novel component designs are introduced that fall outside the model's training distribution. Additionally, if the robotic system's control loop relies on continuously updated models or transfer learning from one facility type to another (e.g., power to enrichment), the domain shift can silently degrade performance without triggering requalification, and version control across distributed construction sites becomes a pipeline integrity nightmare.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: sensitivity to designs outside trained scope
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Model inference failures during remote handling or robotic construction tasks could result in physical collisions, dropped loads, or mis-positioned safety-critical components, with consequences compounded by the system's direct physical actuation authority. The ML pipeline's reliance on static training datasets and weak requalification triggers means degraded performance accumulates silently across construction phases and facility types.

security_specialist.argument: AI-guided robotics in design and construction create a high-value insider target: an adversary with credential access could subtly retask robots to mis-install critical components (e.g., misalign seals in enrichment cascades, weaken structural welds in reactor containment) in ways that pass visual inspection but create latent vulnerabilities exploitable during operations. The physical actuation capability means compromise translates directly to sabotage without requiring the insider to physically touch controlled equipment, reducing detection risk. Facilities spanning power generation, enrichment, and reprocessing magnify this risk because a single compromised robotic control interface could be replicated across multiple high-consequence domains, and because construction-phase tampering is harder to attribute post-facto than operational anomalies.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Adversaries gain a credential-mediated pathway to embed latent physical defects in safety-critical infrastructure during construction, with sabotage effects delayed until operational stressors activate the weaknesses, complicating forensic attribution and bypassing traditional physical access controls.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Licensing documentation is foundational for demonstrating compliance with safety limits, design bases, and operational controls across multiple facility types. ai_engineer.argument: Generative models for licensing documentation face acute data provenance and quality challenges because training data must span decades of evolving regulatory language, facility-specific technical specifications, and jurisdiction-dependent compliance frameworks. Operational drift is a structural problem because regulatory requirements evolve continuously while model retraining cycles are infrequent, creating a widening gap between what the model learned and current compliance standards. security_specialist.argument: This use case creates a concentrated high-value target: compromise of the AI system or its training pipeline allows an adversary to systematically inject compliance-acceptable language that masks proliferation-relevant omissions or creates exploitable ambiguities across multiple facility types. The consequence is not immediate radiological release but potential fuel performance degradation (clad breach, fission gas release) or subcriticality margin erosion if many pellets deviate systematically, compounded if the AI's recommendations subtly maximize throughput at the expense of these hidden quality margins.

use_case: Automated detection of discrepancies between design-basis accident scenarios and actual facility configuration changes
incurred_insecurity: Undetected configuration changes may invalidate design-basis accident analyses, allowing the facility to operate outside analyzed safety envelopes until an upset reveals that actual consequences exceed licensing commitments. This risk is amplified when adversaries exploit the system as a single point of compromise to mask unauthorized modifications supporting diversion, while automated detection erodes the multilayered human verification culture that previously defended against such changes.

nuclear_engineer.argument: In a reprocessing facility, design-basis accidents often involve criticality scenarios, radionuclide release pathways, and solvent fire propagation that are tightly coupled to physical configuration (tank geometry, pipe routing, ventilation damper states, criticality controls). If an AI tool fails to flag a discrepancy—say, a new transfer line that creates an unanalyzed criticality geometry or a ventilation modification that invalidates confinement assumptions—operators and licensees may proceed under the belief that the design basis still bounds the facility. The consequence is not immediate: it manifests when an upset occurs and the actual facility response deviates from analyzed safety limits, potentially exceeding dose consequences or challenging confinement. Existing practice relies on human review of modification packages against the safety analysis report, so this AI acts as a screening layer; if it hallucinates compliance or misses a subtle change (e.g., a valve re-designation that alters flow paths), the traditional review may also miss it due to automation bias.

nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Undetected configuration changes may invalidate design-basis accident analyses, allowing the facility to operate outside analyzed safety envelopes until an upset reveals that actual consequences (criticality margin, confinement performance, dose release) exceed licensing commitments—at which point procedural and physical safeguards predicated on the old analysis no longer apply.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case depends on ingesting structured configuration change records (as-built drawings, modification packages, maintenance logs) and comparing them against design-basis accident scenario documentation—both likely semi-structured text and diagrams with inconsistent schemas across reprocessing facilities. Data provenance is critical: if the system is trained on one facility's documentation format or nomenclature and deployed at another, transfer-learning mismatch will cause missed discrepancies. Reprocessing facilities undergo continuous modification (hot-cell reconfigurations, criticality control geometry changes, solvent extraction parameter updates), creating rapid operational drift where the model's understanding of 'normal' configuration states becomes stale. At inference time, the system must reconcile multi-use acronyms (e.g., 'PUREX' referring to process chemistry vs. facility subsystem) and detect semantically equivalent but textually distinct descriptions of the same physical change, making it vulnerable to mistranslation. The architecture likely relies on document embeddings or entity-extraction pipelines that have no mechanism to flag when input configuration data describes equipment or processes genuinely outside the training distribution, leading to silent failures in discrepancy detection.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: mistranslation or misattribution of multi-use acronyms
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Silent failure to detect configuration changes that invalidate design-basis accident assumptions occurs when the model encounters facility-specific documentation formats, nomenclature drift from continuous modifications, or semantically ambiguous descriptions of physical changes that fall outside its training distribution, with no reliable out-of-distribution detection mechanism at inference time.

security_specialist.argument: In a reprocessing facility, this AI system creates a concentrated point of adversarial leverage: if an insider or nation-state actor can compromise the discrepancy-detection logic or its input feeds, they gain a regulatory 'all-clear' mechanism that masks unauthorized configuration changes supporting material diversion or process modification. The system's reliance on design-basis documentation and live configuration data creates dual attack vectors—poison the reference documents during updates, or manipulate the facility data stream to hide changes already made. An adversary timing a diversion campaign would prioritize blinding this watchdog first, because automated detection lulls both operators and regulators into trusting that discrepancies *would* be caught, reducing manual cross-checks. The concentration of discrepancy-detection authority in one system means compromising it is more efficient than evading multiple independent human reviews, and a sophisticated actor (especially state-level with long timelines) could pre-position subtle biases during the AI's training or deployment phases that only activate under specific configurations tied to diversion-relevant modifications.
proposed_vulnerability_terms: inability to detect unique or contrived component modifications
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: An adversary gains a high-value single point of compromise that, if successfully manipulated, provides regulatory cover for unauthorized facility modifications supporting diversion pathways, while simultaneously eroding the multilayered human verification culture that previously defended against such changes.
